title: Webhook-first hosted inference: messaging & rate experiments
body:
Context:
This is a working brief for a webhook-first quickstart and pricing language experiment aimed at developer teams that integrate event-driven inference (webhooks, background workers, real-time triggers). Goal is to test whether framing Hosted API as a low-friction, event-native service increases activation and early usage velocity for infra/platform customers and engineers building automation features.

Objectives:
- Create 3 distinct messaging angles and microcopy for the quickstart flow (button text, onboarding step titles, email follow-ups).
- Draft pricing language that speaks to event-driven patterns (burst buffers, cold-start mitigation, per-inference vs per-token clarity).
- Sketch the competitive differentiation vs 3 proximate players (general inference APIs, managed endpoint vendors, and serverless function + GPU offerings).
- Define 2 A/B tests and success metrics for a 6-week pilot.

Target audience:
- Backend engineers building automation (webhooks, connectors, moderation pipelines).
- Platform/infra engineers evaluating a managed inference alternative to self-hosting.
- Growth-stage product teams shipping prototypes where cost predictability matters.

Core value props to highlight (developer-first lens):
1) Plug-and-run webhooks: one-line setup to receive and respond to events (example: GitHub -> Redwood webhook -> inference -> app). Emphasize 5–10 minute integration with code sample.
2) Pay-for-outcomes pricing: predictable per-inference buckets plus optional burst credits to cover spiky event workloads. Remove ambiguity around tokens for webhook use-cases (short prompt + generation).
3) Autoscaling with graceful fallback: automatic scaling between latency SLO and cost tier; transparent fallback to a cheaper model variant when capacity limited.
4) Observability for events: per-endpoint traces show latency and cost per webhook invocation, sample payloads in Console.

Quickstart angles (three variants):
A — "One webhook to prod": emphasize minimal config, starter template repo, 3-line server snippet, and a free 48-hour burst credit for first 10k inferences. Microcopy: CTA: "Create webhook". Onboarding step: "Drop in our sample and hit send."
B — "Event processing, predictable spend": emphasize per-inference pricing tiers with an estimator in the onboarding flow. Microcopy: CTA: "Estimate my bill". Onboarding step: "Paste your event rate, we’ll size burst allowance."
C — "Safe defaults for automation": emphasize default caching and prefix-KV that reduces repeated prompt costs; built-in content-safety hooks. Microcopy: CTA: "Start safely." Onboarding step: "Enable safety and caching (recommended)."

Pricing-language drafts (experiment snippets):
- Headline: "Pay per call, scale without surprises."
- Short explainer: "For webhook-driven workflows we charge per inference call and per output token. To simplify planning, each integration gets an option to buy ‘burst credits’ that cover short spikes at a reduced unit rate — automatically applied before your standard usage charges."
- Two example lines to test in UI: 1) "Estimated cost per 1k webhook calls: $X — includes 200k tokens of output"; 2) "Reserve a burst pack: 100k calls for $Y (best for spiky traffic)."
- Note: Include a FAQ entry: "How tokens are counted for webhooks" that briefly explains input vs output tokens, dynamic prompt templates, and caching.

Competitive notes (short primer):
- Competitor A (large API provider): strongest brand + low friction; weakness: opaque cost for bursts, limited per-route observability. Our angle: clearer event billing and better per-webhook visibility.
- Competitor B (managed endpoints): good for large model SLAs; weakness: onboarding friction and lack of event templates. Our angle: templated webhook starters + free burst credits to remove friction.
- Competitor C (serverless + self-hosted inference): cheaper at scale but high ops burden and poor latency guarantees. Our angle: managed autoscaling + fallbacks to control cost without losing reliability.

Objections and rebuttals (developer focused):
- "I can just self-host on GPU spot instances": Rebuttal: "Spot + orchestration needs engineering cycles; we show end-to-end cost, latency SLOs, and a predictable fallthrough plan — plus exportable usage logs for audits."
- "I need fine-grained cost control": "We provide per-route budgets, burst packs, and token estimators during onboarding; you can pin a model and a cost profile per webhook."
- "Request volume is too spiky for hosted pricing": "Burst credits and automatic fallback to cheaper model variants keep costs bounded; we surface per-call cost so you can set alerts and caps."

A/B test proposals (two experiments):
1) CTA language test across 12k new signups: "Create webhook" vs "Estimate my bill". Primary metric: 7-day activation (first successful webhook call). Secondary: 14-day spend. Hypothesis: billing transparency reduces drop-off for infra teams.
2) Onboarding credit test across 8k teams: 48-hour burst vs 3-day $50 trial credit. Primary metric: median number of calls in first 72 hours. Secondary: retention at 30 days. Hypothesis: guaranteed short burst increases initial usage velocity; monetary credit improves retention.

Tracking & dashboards:
- Console funnel: sign-up -> create-hook -> first-call -> first-1000-calls.
- Observe per-route CP50/CP95 latency, cost/call, tokens/call, cache-hit %.
- Jira tickets to instrument: GM-5821 (billing estimator), GM-5823 (webhook templates), GM-5830 (burst pack UI).

Microcopy examples (for dev docs & UI):
- Empty state: "No webhooks yet — connect a source in minutes. Try the GitHub starter."
- Error: "Invocation failed — check payload size (max 512KB) or enable retry."
- Pricing hint: "Estimated per-1k calls: $X (includes average 50 output tokens). Use ‘Estimate’ to refine for your workload."

Next steps & owners:
- Week 1: implement two quickstart templates (GitHub webhook, Slack slash command) — owner: Sam O'Neill.
- Week 2: mock-up onboarding flows and billing estimator — owner: Priya Desai.
- Week 3: instrument A/B tests and QA in beta org — owner: Marco Gutierrez.
- Week 4–6: run pilot, collect metrics, iterate messaging.

Open questions (to resolve before launch):
- Bursts: how to price burst packs (flat vs tiered)? finance input required (ping: finance@redwood).
- Token counting edge cases for templated prompts — engineering to confirm (see jira GM-5821).
- Legal: acceptable use and content-safety wording for automated event processing.

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep developer copy concise, example-first.
- Default to safe, conservative cost estimator numbers in UI; surface an advanced estimator for technical teams.
- Run copy through a short VO test with 10 sales calls and 5 prospects in developer roles.

References and links:
- Starter repo: github.com/redwood-inference/webhook-starters (draft)
- Confluence brief: confluence.redwood.com/display/GT/Webhook+Quickstart+Plan
- Slack thread: #gtm-hosted-api (pinned messages Aug–Nov 2025)

End of brief. This is intentionally terse — use as the central doc for copy drafts and experiments. Iterate in-place and synchronize with product for pricing decisions before UI changes.
